flashcards.back: Hydrogen in palladium

flashcards.front: Solid solution with a **liquid** as solute?
flashcards.back: Amalgam of mercury with sodium

flashcards.front: Gaseous solutions with a liquid and a solid solute (NCERT examples)?
flashcards.back: Chloroform mixed with N$_2$ (liquid in gas); camphor in N$_2$ (solid in gas)

Moles of solute per litre of **solution**; mol L$^{-1}$

flashcards.front: Which concentration units do not depend on temperature?
flashcards.back: Mass %, ppm, mole fraction, molality (only masses / moles)

flashcards.front: Why does molarity change with temperature?
flashcards.back: It contains the volume of the solution, which changes with temperature.
Grams of solute in 100 mL of solution (used in medicine; normal saline is 0.9% w/V NaCl)
$\dfrac{	ext{parts of component}}{	ext{total parts}} 	imes 10^6$

flashcards.front: Mole fraction of solute in a 1 molal aqueous solution

flashcards.back: Solubility of a gas ∝ its partial pressure (constant T); or $p = K_Hx$ - partial pressure ∝ mole fraction in solution.
Lower solubility ($x = p/K_H$)
It increases - gases become less soluble as temperature rises.

flashcards.front: Why does gas solubility fall with rising temperature?
flashcards.back: Dissolution of a gas is exothermic; by Le Chatelier's principle heating shifts the equilibrium back to free gas.
N$_2$ dissolved in blood at high pressure forms bubbles when a diver surfaces, blocking capillaries.
Low blood O$_2$ at high altitude (low partial pressure of O$_2$): weakness, unable to think clearly.

flashcards.front: Effect of pressure on the solubility of a solid in a liquid
flashcards.back: No significant effect - solids and liquids are nearly incompressible.
Partial vapour pressure of each component ∝ its mole fraction: $p_i = x_ip_i^\circ$

flashcards.front: $p_{	ext{total}}$ for an ideal binary solution
flashcards.back: $p_1^\circ + (p_2^\circ - p_1^\circ)x_2$

flashcards.front: Mole fraction of a component in the vapour
flashcards.back: $y_i = p_i/p_{	ext{total}}$ (vapour is richer in the more volatile component)

flashcards.front: Raoult's law as a special case of Henry's law
flashcards.back: Both: partial pressure ∝ mole fraction; Raoult's law is Henry's law with $K_H = p_1^\circ$.

flashcards.front: Why does a non-volatile solute lower vapour pressure?
flashcards.back: Solute particles take up part of the surface, so fewer solvent molecules escape.
Obeys Raoult's law at all concentrations; $\Delta_{mix}H = 0$; $\Delta_{mix}V = 0$
n-hexane + n-heptane; bromoethane + chloroethane; benzene + toluene
Both positive (endothermic, volume increases)
Both negative (exothermic, volume decreases)
Ethanol + acetone; carbon disulphide + acetone
Phenol + aniline; chloroform + acetone

flashcards.front: Why does ethanol + acetone deviate positively?
flashcards.back: Acetone breaks some hydrogen bonds between ethanol molecules, weakening the interactions.

flashcards.front: Why does chloroform + acetone deviate negatively?
flashcards.back: Chloroform's H hydrogen bonds to acetone's carbonyl oxygen - stronger A-B attraction.
Binary mixture with the same composition in liquid and vapour, boiling at constant temperature; cannot be separated by fractional distillation.

flashcards.front: Minimum boiling azeotrope: deviation and example
flashcards.back: Large positive deviation; ethanol-water (about 95% ethanol by volume)

flashcards.front: Maximum boiling azeotrope: deviation and example
flashcards.back: Large negative deviation; HNO$_3$-water (68% HNO$_3$, 32% water by mass, 393.5 K)
Depends on the number of solute particles, not their nature, relative to total particles in solution.
Relative lowering of vapour pressure, elevation of b.p., depression of f.p., osmotic pressure

flashcards.front: Relative lowering of vapour pressure equals...
flashcards.back: The mole fraction of the solute: $(p_1^\circ - p_1)/p_1^\circ = x_2$
$\dfrac{p_1^\circ - p_1}{p_1^\circ} = \dfrac{w_2M_1}{M_2w_1}$

flashcards.front: Why does a solution boil at a higher temperature?
flashcards.back: Its vapour pressure is lower, so it must be heated more to reach atmospheric pressure.
$\Delta T_b = K_bm$; boiling point elevation / molal elevation / ebullioscopic constant
$\Delta T_f = K_fm$; freezing point depression / molal depression / cryoscopic constant
Temperature at which the vapour pressure of the liquid phase equals that of the solid phase.

flashcards.front: $K_f$ in terms of enthalpy of fusion
flashcards.back: $K_f = \dfrac{RM_1T_f^2}{1000\,\Delta_{fus}H}$

flashcards.front: Boiling point of 1 mol sucrose in 1000 g water
flashcards.back: NCERT states 373.52 K (= 373 + 0.52). With $\Delta T_b = K_bm$ and 373.15 K the equation gives 373.67 K - see lesson 7.1. In calculations use 373.15 K unless the question says otherwise.
Flow of solvent through a semipermeable membrane from pure solvent (or dilute solution) into solution (or concentrated solution).
Excess pressure that must be applied to a solution to prevent osmosis.
$\pi = CRT$ ($C$ = molarity); $M_2 = w_2RT/\pi V$

flashcards.front: Three advantages of the osmotic pressure method
flashcards.back: Room temperature; uses molarity; large value even for very dilute solutions - ideal for proteins and polymers.
Same osmotic pressure at the same temperature; no osmosis between them.
0.9% (mass/volume) NaCl - isotonic with the fluid in blood cells

flashcards.front: Cells in hypertonic vs hypotonic solution
flashcards.back: Hypertonic (> 0.9% NaCl): shrink. Hypotonic (< 0.9%): swell.
Pressure larger than π on the solution side pushes pure solvent out through the membrane; used for desalination.
Cellulose acetate film on a support
Puffiness from water retained in tissues by osmosis when a lot of salt is eaten.

flashcards.front: Why do salted meat and candied fruit resist bacteria?
flashcards.back: Bacteria lose water by osmosis, shrivel and die.
Experimental molar mass lower (dissociation) or higher (association) than the normal value.
normal M / abnormal M = observed / calculated colligative property = moles of particles after / before
Dissociation; association

flashcards.front: Why does ethanoic acid have $i \approx 0.5$ in benzene?
flashcards.back: It dimerises through hydrogen bonding (low dielectric constant solvent).
$\alpha = (i - 1)/(n - 1)$, $n$ = ions per formula unit
$i = 1 - \alpha/2$, so $\alpha = 2(1 - i)$
